exam.topic: Discrete random variable

paragraphs: The distribution function (d.f.) of the discrete random variable \(Y\) (\(F(y)\)) is plotted below:
parts: i) Write the equation for the probability function (p.f.) of \(Y\) (\(f(y)\)) that is associated with the d.f. shown above. The equation must completely define \(f(y)\) for all values of \(y\).
ii) What is the probability that \(Y > 0\)?
iii) What is the probability that \(0.5 < Y < 3.75\)?

solution.title: Read the jumps of the d.f.
solution.words: The d.f. is flat everywhere except at the values that \(Y\) can take. The filled circle marks the value of \(F(y)\) at a jump. The height of each jump is the probability of that value.

solution.title: Part i. Write the probability function
solution.words: The p.f. lists every value with a jump and is 0 elsewhere. The probabilities add to 1, so the function is completely defined.

solution.title: Part ii. From the d.f.
solution.words: \(F(0)\) is read from the flat part of the plot that covers \(y=0\).

solution.title: Part ii. From the p.f.
solution.words: Adding the probabilities of the values above the bound gives the same answer.

solution.title: Part iii. From the d.f.
solution.words: \(Y\) has no probability at \(y=3.75\), so \(P(Y<3.75)=F(3.75)\).

solution.title: Part iii. From the p.f.
solution.words: Only the values of \(Y\) strictly between the two bounds are counted.

exam.topic: Continuous random variable
exam.title: Density that rises in a straight line
paragraphs: The probability density function (p.d.f.) of the continuous random variable \(X\) is:
parts: i) What is the expected value of the random variable \(X\) (i.e., what is \(E[X]\))?
ii) Write the equation for the distribution function (d.f.) (\(F(x)\)) of \(X\) that is associated with the p.d.f. above. The equation must completely define \(F(x)\) for all values of \(x\).
iii) What is the 25th percentile of the random variable \(X\)?

solution.title: Part i. Expected value
solution.words: The density is 0 outside \(0<x\le 6\), so only the middle integral contributes.

solution.title: Part ii. The d.f. for x at or below 0
solution.words: No probability has accumulated before the density starts.

solution.title: Part ii. The d.f. inside the interval
solution.words: The dummy variable \(u\) is used inside the integral because \(x\) is the upper limit.

solution.title: Part ii. The d.f. above 6
solution.words: All of the probability has accumulated by \(x=6\), so the d.f. stays at 1.

solution.title: Part ii. Complete distribution function
solution.words: The three pieces together define \(F(x)\) for all values of \(x\).

solution.title: Part iii. The 25th percentile
solution.words: The d.f. passes 0.25 inside the range 0 to 6, so the middle piece is used. The positive root is the percentile.

exam.conclusion: \(E[X]=4\). \(F(x)=0\) for \(x\le 0\), \(F(x)=x^{2}/36\) for \(0<x\le 6\) and \(F(x)=1\) for \(x>6\). The 25th percentile of \(X\) is 3.

exam.topic: Sampling distribution of the mean
exam.title: Pure-tone average in older adults
paragraphs: The pure-tone average (PTA, the mean of the hearing thresholds at 500, 1000, 2000 and 4000 Hz) is a commonly used marker of hearing sensitivity. In the population of adults in the U.S. between 60 and 69 years of age, PTA is Normally distributed with mean of 28 dB HL and standard deviation of 12 dB HL.
parts: What is the probability that the mean value of PTA in a sample of 36 adults in this age range is between 26 and 31 dB HL?

solution.title: Define the random variable
solution.words: PTA in one person is a Normally distributed random variable. Call it \(X\).

solution.title: Distribution of the sample mean
general: \bar X\sim N\left(\mu_{\bar X},\sigma_{\bar X}^{2}\right),\quad \mu_{\bar X}=\mu,\quad \sigma_{\bar X}=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}
solution.words: The mean of a sample of 36 is also a random variable. It has the same mean as \(X\) and a smaller standard deviation, called the standard error of the mean.

solution.title: Convert to the Standard Normal
general: P(a<\bar X<b)=P\left(\frac{a-\mu_{\bar X}}{\sigma_{\bar X}}<Z<\frac{b-\mu_{\bar X}}{\sigma_{\bar X}}\right)
solution.words: The standard error is used in the denominator because the question is about a sample mean and not about one person.

solution.title: Read the z table
solution.words: The z table lists only positive z values. The Normal curve is symmetric, so the area below \(-1.00\) equals the area above \(1.00\). The printed values are \(F(1.00)=0.8413\) and \(F(1.50)=0.9332\).

exam.conclusion: The probability that the mean PTA in a sample of 36 adults in this age range is between 26 and 31 dB HL is 0.7745.

exam.topic: One-way ANOVA from summary statistics
exam.title: Sound therapy for tinnitus
paragraphs: A study was reported concerning the effect of sound therapy on tinnitus (a ringing or buzzing sound that is heard when no outside sound is present). Adults with chronic tinnitus volunteering for the study were randomized to one of three treatment groups: Group 1 - notched music, which is music with the frequency band around the tinnitus pitch removed (\(n = 12\)); Group 2 - broadband noise (\(n = 12\)); Group 3 - counseling only (\(n = 12\)). The subjects were seen every month for a 3-month period. The reduction in tinnitus loudness was measured for each subject by loudness matching (expressed in decibels, dB) and was found to be Normally distributed. The mean and standard deviation are given below for each group.
parts: Based on these data, is there a difference in the reduction in tinnitus loudness among these three groups? Use a significance level of \(\alpha = 0.05\) for your inference. (Note: If a difference exists, do not identify which groups are different.)

solution.title: Statistical test
solution.words: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA). There are more than 2 groups made up of different subjects. The data are interval (continuous) and are Normally distributed.

solution.title: Null hypothesis
solution.words: There is no difference in mean reduction in tinnitus loudness among the subjects in these three groups.

solution.title: Group counts
general: m=\text{number of groups},\quad n=\text{number within each group}
solution.words: Every group has the same size, so the balanced formulas apply.

solution.title: Within groups variance
solution.words: The within groups variance is the average of the three sample variances. Each standard deviation is squared first.

solution.title: Grand mean
solution.words: The grand mean is the mean of the three group means because the groups are the same size.

solution.title: Variance of the group means
solution.words: This is the square of the standard error of the mean, estimated from how far the group means lie from the grand mean.

solution.title: Between groups variance
solution.words: Multiplying by the group size turns the variance of the means into an estimate of the population variance.

solution.title: F value
solution.words: F is near 1 when the null hypothesis is true and becomes large when the group means are spread apart.

solution.title: Degrees of freedom
solution.words: The numerator degrees of freedom come from the number of groups. The denominator degrees of freedom come from the subjects within the groups.

solution.title: Critical value
solution.words: The F table has no row for \(\nu_d=33\). The printed rows 32 and 34 bracket it. The larger value from row 32 is used as the cutoff because it is the conservative choice.

solution.title: Comparison
solution.words: F is larger than the critical value at \(\alpha=0.05\), so the null hypothesis is rejected. F is also larger than the boldface value for 0.01, so the P range is \(P<0.01\).

exam.conclusion: Reject the null hypothesis. There is a significant difference in reduction in tinnitus loudness among these three groups with \(P<0.01\).

exam.topic: Chi-square test on a contingency table
exam.title: Nerve stimulator for migraine attacks
paragraphs: A study done at a headache center sought to evaluate the efficacy of a nerve stimulator worn on the forehead versus the more standard treatment of a migraine tablet or a sham (inactive) stimulator for stopping a migraine attack (a severe throbbing headache, often with nausea and sensitivity to light). Subjects were randomized into one of three treatment arms and were assessed for freedom from pain two hours after treating their next attack. The results of the study can be found in the table below:
parts: Based on this sample, is there a difference in rates of freedom from pain among the different treatment groups? Use a significance level of \(\alpha = 0.05\) for your inference. (Note: If you do find a difference, do not isolate differences.)

solution.title: Statistical test
solution.words: \(\chi^{2}\) test. The data are nominal counts in a 2x3 contingency table.

solution.title: Null hypothesis
solution.words: There is no difference in the rates of freedom from pain among the three treatment groups.

solution.title: Row and column totals
general: R_i=\text{total of row }i,\quad C_j=\text{total of column }j,\quad n=\text{grand total}
solution.words: The totals are the ones printed in the margins of the table.

solution.title: Expected values under the null hypothesis
solution.words: Here \(i\) refers to the row and \(j\) refers to the column. Each expected count is the count that would be seen if every group had the same overall rate.

solution.title: Chi-square statistic
solution.words: One term is calculated for each of the six cells and the terms are added.

solution.title: Degrees of freedom
solution.words: The totals row and the totals column are not counted.

solution.title: Critical value
solution.words: Start with \(\alpha=0.05\). The value is read from the chi-square table in row 2 and the column for an upper tail area of 0.050.

solution.title: Comparison
solution.words: The statistic is larger than the critical value at \(\alpha=0.05\), so the null hypothesis is rejected. The stricter columns of the table are then checked in turn. The smallest printed level that is still exceeded is 0.001, so \(P<0.001\).

exam.conclusion: Reject the null hypothesis. There is a difference in the rates of freedom from pain among the three treatment groups with \(P<0.001\).

paragraphs: To study if listening to loud music through headphones is associated with an increased chance of high-frequency hearing loss, young adults with high-frequency hearing loss from a university audiology clinic's database served as cases in a retrospective case-control study. parts: A \(\chi^{2}\)-test has been performed and it was found that there is a difference in having high-frequency hearing loss between the loud headphone listener and non-listener groups (p<0.01).

Quantify the degree of association between having high-frequency hearing loss and listening to loud music through headphones. Provide your result in a single complete sentence that would convey your conclusion in a way that could be understood by a non-expert in statistics or medicine (e.g., a typical reader of a local newspaper).

solution.title: Statistical analysis
solution.words: This was a retrospective case-control study, so an Odds Ratio is calculated (not a Relative Risk). The cases were chosen because they already had the condition, so the risk in each exposure group cannot be estimated.

solution.title: Label the table
solution.words: E is exposed and U is unexposed. D is with the condition (the cases) and N is without the condition (the controls).

solution.title: Calculate the Odds Ratio
general: OR=\frac{\text{odds of cases in those exposed}}{\text{odds of cases in those not exposed}}=\frac{n_{ED}/n_{EN}}{n_{UD}/n_{UN}}=\frac{n_{ED}\cdot n_{UN}}{n_{UD}\cdot n_{EN}}
solution.words: The odds ratio is rounded to one or two figures for the sentence because a newspaper reader does not need more.

exam.conclusion: The odds of having high-frequency hearing loss are about 1.9 times greater for young adults who listen to loud music through headphones compared to those who do not.

exam.topic: Two-sample t test from summary statistics
exam.title: Live tutors and song learning in zebra finches
paragraphs: Researchers interested in how young songbirds learn to sing did a study in zebra finches. Juvenile males were divided into two groups: 14 birds were raised with a live adult tutor (live tutor group) and 18 birds heard recordings of the same tutors through a loudspeaker (loudspeaker group). When the birds were adults, the similarity of each bird's song to the song of its tutor was scored (percent of tutor syllables that were copied). The live tutor group had \(\bar{x}_1 = 71.4\) and \(s_1 = 9.8\); the loudspeaker group had \(\bar{x}_2 = 60.2\) and \(s_2 = 11.6\).
parts: Can the researchers conclude that there is a difference in song similarity scores between the two tutoring populations? Use the appropriate statistical test that is formulated for only two groups. You can assume that these interval data are Normally distributed.

solution.title: Statistical test
solution.words: Two-sample t Test (also called the unpaired t Test or independent samples t Test). There are two groups made up of different subjects and the data are interval and Normally distributed.

solution.title: Null hypothesis
solution.words: There is no difference in song similarity scores between the two tutoring groups.

solution.title: Given values
general: n_1,\ \bar x_1,\ s_1\qquad n_2,\ \bar x_2,\ s_2
solution.words: The values are in percent. The two groups have different sizes, so the pooled variance must weight each sample variance by its degrees of freedom.

solution.title: Pooled variance
solution.words: The pooled variance lies between the two sample variances and is closer to the variance of the larger group.

solution.title: t statistic
solution.words: The denominator is the standard error of the difference between the two sample means.

solution.title: Degrees of freedom
solution.words: One degree of freedom is lost for each sample mean.

solution.title: Critical value
solution.words: Start with \(\alpha=0.05\). The t table has a row for \(\nu=30\).

solution.title: Comparison
solution.words: \(|t|\) is larger than the critical value at 0.05, so the null hypothesis is rejected. The stricter columns are then checked in turn. The smallest printed level that is still exceeded is 0.01.

exam.conclusion: Reject the null hypothesis and conclude that there is a difference in song similarity scores between the two tutoring groups (\(P<0.01\)).

solution.words: The pooled proportion uses all of the children together because the null hypothesis says that the two groups share one proportion.

solution.title: z statistic
solution.words: The term subtracted in the numerator is the Yates correction for continuity.

solution.title: Critical value
solution.words: Start with \(\alpha=0.05\). The critical z value is read from the infinity row of the two-tailed t table.

solution.title: Comparison
solution.words: \(|z|\) is larger than the critical value at 0.05, so the null hypothesis is rejected. It is smaller than the critical value at 0.02, so the P range is \(P<0.05\).

exam.conclusion: There is a significant difference between the proportion of children with an older sibling who pass the false-belief task and the proportion of children with no older sibling who pass it, with \(P<0.05\).

exam.topic: Bonferroni pairwise t tests after ANOVA
exam.title: Three treatments for amblyopia
paragraphs: Amblyopia (reduced vision in one eye because the brain favors the other eye) is usually treated in childhood by making the child use the weaker eye. A study was designed to examine the effect of three different treatments. Children with amblyopia were randomized into three different treatment groups (\(n = 12\) for each group), and after 16 weeks of treatment each child's improvement in visual acuity was measured as the number of additional letters read on an eye chart with the weaker eye. The results are summarized in the table below.
An ANOVA test demonstrated that the \(F\) test-statistic is significant at \(\alpha = 0.05\) (\(F = 4.0233\), \(P < 0.05\)), with a value of \(s^{2}_{wit} = 17.7267\).
You will need \(t_{0.0167}(33)\). The R command and its result are shown below.
parts: Using the appropriate pairwise comparison method and the Bonferroni correction, determine which treatment groups result in differences in visual acuity improvement.

solution.title: Statistical test
solution.words: Multiple (three) unpaired t Tests with the Bonferroni correction.

solution.title: Null hypothesis
solution.words: There is no difference in visual acuity improvement between Group 1 (Eye Patch) and Group 2 (Blurring Eye Drops), AND no difference between Group 1 (Eye Patch) and Group 3 (Video Game), AND no difference between Group 2 (Blurring Eye Drops) and Group 3 (Video Game).

solution.title: Given values
solution.words: The within groups variance from the ANOVA is used for every pair. Its degrees of freedom are the denominator degrees of freedom of the ANOVA.

solution.title: Pairwise t statistics
solution.words: Every pair uses the same denominator because the groups are the same size.

solution.title: Bonferroni level of significance
solution.words: There are three pairwise comparisons. Every comparison is tested at the same corrected level.

solution.title: Critical value
solution.words: The printed t table has no column for 0.0167, so the value from the supplied R result is used. It lies between the printed values for 0.02 and 0.01 in row 33, as it should.

solution.title: Comparisons
solution.words: There is no difference between the Eye Patch and Blurring Eye Drops groups. There is a difference between the Eye Patch and Video Game groups. There is no difference between the Blurring Eye Drops and Video Game groups.

exam.conclusion: There is no difference in mean visual acuity improvement between Group 1 (Eye Patch) and Group 2 (Blurring Eye Drops), or between Group 2 (Blurring Eye Drops) and Group 3 (Video Game), but there is a difference in mean visual acuity improvement between Group 1 (Eye Patch) and Group 3 (Video Game). This entire statement is made with \(P<0.05\).

exam.topic: 2x2 chi-square test with Yates correction and relative risk
exam.title: Prior concussion and a new concussion in football
paragraphs: The following data were taken from a prospective study of 830 high school football players. At the start of the season the players were given questionnaires about their medical history, including whether or not they had ever had a concussion (a mild brain injury caused by a blow to the head). During the season the players were followed by athletic trainers and evaluated for a new concussion, with the following results:
parts: i) Use a \(\chi^{2}\) test to determine if there is a difference in the occurrence of a new concussion between the players with a prior concussion and the players with no prior concussion.

ii) If there is a difference, quantify the degree of association between a player's having a prior concussion and the occurrence of a new concussion during the season. Provide your result in a single complete sentence that would convey your conclusion in a way that could be understood by a non-expert in statistics or medicine (e.g., a typical reader of a local newspaper).

solution.title: Part i. Statistical test
solution.words: \(\chi^{2}\) test. The data are nominal counts in a 2x2 contingency table, so the Yates continuity correction is used.

solution.title: Part i. Null hypothesis
solution.words: There is no difference in the occurrence of a new concussion between players with a prior concussion and players with no prior concussion.

solution.title: Part i. Row and column totals
general: R_i=\text{total of row }i,\quad C_j=\text{total of column }j,\quad n=\text{grand total}
solution.words: The totals are not printed in the table, so they are calculated first.

solution.title: Part i. Expected values under the null hypothesis
solution.words: Here \(i\) refers to the row and \(j\) refers to the column.

solution.title: Part i. Chi-square statistic with the Yates correction
solution.words: One half is subtracted from the size of every difference before it is squared.

solution.title: Part i. Degrees of freedom
solution.words: A 2x2 table always has 1 degree of freedom.

solution.title: Part i. Critical value
solution.words: Start with \(\alpha=0.05\). The value is read from row 1 of the chi-square table.

solution.title: Part i. Comparison
solution.words: The statistic is larger than the critical value at 0.05, so the null hypothesis is rejected. The stricter columns are then checked in turn. The smallest printed level that is still exceeded is 0.001, so \(P<0.001\). There is a difference in the occurrence of a new concussion between the two groups.

solution.title: Part ii. Choose the measure of association
solution.words: The data are from a prospective study, so a Relative Risk can be calculated. The exposure of interest is a prior concussion and the event is a new concussion. T marks the exposed group and C marks the comparison group.

solution.title: Part ii. Relative Risk
general: RR=\frac{\text{probability of event in treatment group}}{\text{probability of event in control group}}=\frac{n_{TD}/n_T}{n_{CD}/n_C}
solution.words: The relative risk is rounded for the sentence because a newspaper reader does not need more figures.

exam.conclusion: Reject the null hypothesis and conclude that there is a difference in the occurrence of a new concussion between players with a prior concussion and players with no prior concussion (\(P<0.001\)). The risk of a new concussion during the season is about 2.3 times greater for players who have had a prior concussion compared to players who have not.

notes: All data are invented for practice. No result is a real study's finding.

Types R1 to R5 are the reviewed-but-not-tested homework types (R1 two-sample t, R2 one-sample t, R3 z Test for two proportions with Yates, R4 Bonferroni, R5 2x2 chi-square with Yates then relative risk).
T1 and T2 stay abstract like the exam. nx1-03 says in one clause what Y counts.

The question text (paragraphs, parts) keeps the exam and homework wording, including the colons and semicolons of the original stems ('plotted below:', 'treatment groups: Group 1 - ...; Group 2 - ...', 'in the table below:', 'From the ANOVA (performed in R):', 'The results were as follows:', 'divided into two groups:') and the parenthetical '(Note: ...)'. Solution words and conclusions use no colons or semicolons.

T5 uses the Residuals Mean Sq exactly as printed in the R table for s2_wit, as the posted exam solution does. Holm cutoffs for 0.0167 and 0.025 are bracketed by the printed 0.01, 0.02 and 0.05 columns, and every |t| falls clearly outside its bracket. In nx1-17 the Holm procedure stops at the second comparison.

T7 stems state the result of a chi-square test. Each stated P range was checked with the Yates-corrected 2x2 statistic against the printed table. In T7 the sentence that states the chi-square result is the first entry of parts so that it is shown after the table, as on the exam.
T4 and T6 specify alpha = 0.05. When the null hypothesis is rejected the solution also checks stricter printed levels to give the P range.
nx1-11: nu_d = 33 is not a printed F row. Bracketed with rows 32 and 34 and the row 32 values (3.3, 5.34) used as conservative cutoffs.
nx1-16: nu = 45 is not a printed t row. Each Holm cutoff is bracketed with rows 44 and 46 (stricter column at the lower row as the upper bound).
nx1-26: nu = 41 is not a printed t row. Bracketed with rows 40 and 42. |t| is below both, so the decision does not depend on the bracket.

nx1-29: the Bonferroni cutoff t_0.0167(33) is not a printed column. As in the homework, the question supplies the R qt() result (2.522213, checked with SciPy) and the solution also shows the printed bracket 2.445 < t < 2.733.
Chi-square P ranges use the 0.001 column of the printed table (Table 5-7). nx1-18 and nx1-30 exceed it, so P < 0.001. nx1-21 (13.347) is below 13.816, so P < 0.005.
